name: Red light tan myth

lead: Some looksmaxxing and skincare posters say that exposing skin to red or near-infrared light from LED panels or masks before sun or sunbed sessions prepares it to tan faster or deeper. The appearance payoff wanted is a quicker, deeper tan.

The chain proponents suggest is that red light stimulates skin cells in a way that boosts pigment response. Red light therapy (photobiomodulation) has been studied mainly for wound healing and pain, and no published study tests it as a tanning primer. Natural tanning is described as driven by UV acting on melanocytes.

paras: Users run a red-light panel or mask over the skin for a session before UV exposure, often as part of a wider skincare routine. Descriptions come from informal reasoning on forums.

Red light devices are cleared by the FDA for some uses, and some users report mild irritation or pain; long-term skin effects are described as not known. Tanning with UV carries documented risks, including sunburn and increased skin cancer risk.

web.title: Do you tan in a red light therapy bed?

chain: Red or near-infrared light on skin
angle.text: Some posters say red-light devices used before sun or bed sessions prime skin to tan more readily. The idea is that red light stimulates skin cells and boosts pigment response. Red light therapy has been studied for wound healing and pain, and no published study tests it for tanning.

lead: The red light tan claim is the belief, circulated in looksmaxxing and skincare circles, that treating skin with red or near-infrared light before UV exposure primes it to tan more readily or protects it while tanning. The goal is a deeper, more even tan, which many people use to look healthier, leaner and more defined, with the extra hope of less sun damage along the way. Its proponents rely mostly on informal reasoning and product-marketing claims rather than published research.

Red light therapy, also called low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, uses low-power lasers or LEDs in the red and near-infrared range. It has been studied for wound healing, pain, hair loss and mouth sores from chemotherapy, with mixed results, and is marketed for skin rejuvenation.[1][2] The leading explanation for its effects is absorption of the light by an enzyme in mitochondria.[2]

Natural tanning is described by encyclopedic sources as driven by ultraviolet radiation acting on melanocytes: UVA darkens existing melanin briefly, while UVB damage prompts new melanin production that appears days later.[3] Red and near-infrared light contain no UV, and clinics and device sellers that address the question say red light therapy does not itself tan skin.[4] No published clinical study located tests red light as a tan primer or as protection before UV exposure.
infobox: LED or laser red-light panels, masks, beds[1][4]
Red about 630-660 nm, near-infrared about 810-850 nm[4]
No studies found for tan priming

paras: Proponents describe using red or near-infrared panels or masks on the skin in the days or minutes before tanning, in the hope of a faster or deeper tan or of reduced damage from the UV session. The practice has no standard protocol.

Low-level light therapy applies low-power red or near-infrared light to the body surface. Proponents say it supports healing and cell function; evidence is strongest for preventing oral mucositis and some tendon and osteoarthritis pain, tentative for hair loss, and weak or inconclusive for conditions such as back pain, with many studies small and at risk of bias.[2] Some devices are FDA-cleared, and the agency obtained a permanent injunction in 2015 against a company that marketed devices for over 200 diseases.[2] Hungarian physician Endre Mester is credited with discovering the biological effects of low-power laser light in 1967.[2]

Tanning is skin darkening caused mainly by UV from sunlight or tanning lamps. UVA oxidises existing melanin for a rapid but short-lived darkening, and UVB damages skin DNA, triggering melanin production that appears two or three days later and lasts weeks to months, offering roughly SPF 3 of protection.[3] The Fitzpatrick scale (1975) classifies skin by tanning behaviour, from types that burn easily and rarely tan to types that rarely burn.[3] Red light is not described as part of this process; a clinic page says that red light uses visible red and near-infrared wavelengths rather than UV and acts mainly on mitochondria, and that redness after a session reflects vascular flushing, not pigment change.[4]

No studies found for red light as a tanning primer or as protection before UV exposure. Clinical research on red light therapy concerns other outcomes such as wound healing, pain and skin rejuvenation.[2]

Users of red light devices report mild pain or skin irritation, long-term effects on skin and hair are described as unknown, and some devices call for eye protection.[2] UV tanning is associated with sunburn, skin ageing and increased skin cancer risk; a 2010 study reported that frequent tanning bed use roughly tripled melanoma risk, and the WHO, American Cancer Society and US Surgeon General warn about sun and indoor tanning exposure.[3]
